tweets.text:
The most common criticism of Hyperliquid's buyback policy: burning ~99% of fees on HYPE instead of reinvesting in growth is bad capital allocation. That critique assumes Hyperliquid is a company optimizing ROI on retained earnings. 

It isn't. It's a neutral network, and the buyback is the alignment mechanism, not a wasted opportunity.

You need to hold HYPE to build on Hyperliquid.

trade[XYZ] had to buy 500k hyperliquid:native just to become a HIP-3 deployer, before a dollar of their own revenue. 

The AF routes 99% of protocol fees straight into HYPE buybacks. So every dollar of value XYZ generates for the network flows back into the exact token they were required to hold to operate. Their upside isn't just their fee split, it's the appreciation of the entry ticket itself.

That's not "wasted" capital, it's the trust model: a neutral venue can't have a team discretionarily deciding who gets funded out of protocol revenue.

But growth capital isn't gone either. Separate from the fee engine, Hyperliquid still holds roughly $27B in future emissions and community rewards it can deploy and the two times it's actually chosen to spend from that basket are the best evidence for why people should trust them.

▫️The HYPE airdrop, funded entirely outside any VC allocation, is the reason this is one of the only tokens in the space with genuine trust and a famously meritocratic reputation. 

▫️In February, a 1M HYPE grant, worth ~$29M then, ~$83M now, built the HPC. Six months later, that spend sits behind the CFTC publicly committing to bring Hyperliquid onshore, which just repriced the entire forward-looking earnings case for the token.

Two different pools of capital, two different jobs. 

One turns revenue into permanent alignment. The other proves that when discretion is used, it's used well. Neither is Hyperliquid leaving growth on the table. 

You can't grade any of this against normal company capital allocation, either. A normal company doesn't generate ~$1B in annual revenue on a ten-person team.

Hyperliquid.

Perpetual Derivatives aren't a crypto side-quest, they're a better-designed derivative, and that's the whole thesis of this piece from Syncracy Capital (@RyanWatkins_ & @defi_monk), now available on HRC.

No expiries, no strikes, no theta decay. Just linear, continuous leverage that does what it says on the tin — available 24/7, unlike an options chain or an opaque CFD desk. That simplicity is why retail options volume already tops 50% of all U.S. options activity and CFD volume runs $1T+ a month: people want exposure.

The case for DEXs winning this shift comes down to structure. Legacy market infrastructure fragments trading across intermediaries that can't unify margin the way a perp DEX does natively. Hyperliquid alone is running near $1B annualized revenue on ~99% margins with a 12-person team: software economics applied to an exchange.

The number that matters: perp DEXs are still under $40B in fully diluted value against an ~$8T daily options/futures/CFD pool. Capturing even 1% of that volume is a $3-7B annual revenue business for the winners.

For a product trading hundreds of billions in volume, perpetual contracts still don't have a settled answer to the most basic question under U.S. law: are they futures, or are they swaps? 

One federal judge described the exercise as deciding "whether tetrahedrons belong in square or round holes".

In a new comment letter to the SEC and CFTC, @HyperliquidPC argues the fix has been sitting in plain sight: treat qualifying equity perpetuals as security futures, a category both agencies already oversee, and let exchanges compete on execution instead of jurisdiction. 

The stakes: more than $480 billion in perpetual contract volume that's traded on Hyperliquid over the past ten months alone, waiting on a framework that lets it come onshore.

tweets.text:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is now considering whether perpetual contracts should extend to physically deliverable commodities such as crude oil, and the research presented here provides useful data for that evaluation:

1. Perpetual futures perform the same risk-transfer function as dated futures, at lower cost.
2. Perpetual futures open hedging to participants that standard contract sizes don't economically serve.
3. Off-hours perpetual prices deliver usable price discovery, and hedgers can act on it at realistic cost.
4. Perpetual markets show no statistically significant harm to the incumbent markets they reference.
